analysis.one_liner: Abolishes the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the federal agency that polices consumer lending.
analysis.headline: The bill to abolish the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau was introduced with 7 cosponsors in February 2017, sat in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing or vote, and died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau by repealing the 2010 law that created it, restoring the legal landscape as it existed before Dodd-Frank. The CFPB is the agency that supervises banks and nonbank lenders, handles consumer complaints, and enforces rules against abusive credit card, mortgage, payday lending, and debt collection practices. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Senate Banking Committee until the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, credit card issuers, payday and installment lenders, mortgage servicers, and debt collectors would be freed from a single federal watchdog that supervises them and can return money to consumers it finds were cheated. Supporters argued the bureau's rules raise lending costs and restrict access to credit.

how_it_helps.text: Repealing the Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010 eliminates the bureau entirely, removing its supervision and enforcement authority over banks and nonbank financial companies.
The bill restores or revives provisions of law that the 2010 act amended or repealed, unwinding the bureau's jurisdiction over consumer credit markets.

Financial firms subject to CFPB rules would no longer face that agency's examinations, enforcement actions, or rulemaking on credit card fees, overdraft practices, mortgage servicing, and collection of debts.

analysis.who_pays: Everyday borrowers: credit card holders, mortgage borrowers, payday loan customers, and people dealing with debt collectors would lose the federal agency that handles their complaints and enforces rules against abusive lending and collection practices.

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith case for repeal: the CFPB was created with an unusual structure — a single director funded through the Federal Reserve rather than congressional appropriations — and critics argued it was insufficiently accountable and that its rules raised the cost of credit and limited access to it for some borrowers.

Eliminating the bureau entirely, rather than restructuring it, would leave no federal regulator focused on consumer lending across banks and nonbank lenders, so abusive practices in credit cards, mortgages, payday lending, and debt collection would go back to a patchwork of weaker or nonexistent oversight.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered no replacement or restructuring — it abolished the only federal regulator dedicated to consumer financial protection. The gains would flow to regulated firms in the form of fewer rules and lower compliance costs; the costs would fall on borrowers in the form of weaker recourse against abusive fees, lending, and collection practices. On balance, the cost to ordinary consumers is large and the benefit to them is essentially nil, which is consistent with why the bill attracted no Democratic support and never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee in February 2017 and sat there without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Ted Cruz introduced the Repeal CFPB Act on February 14, 2017.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
The bill would repeal the Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010, the title of the Dodd-Frank law that established the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.
Seven Republican senators cosponsored the bill; the original cosponsors were Senators Lee, Paul, Inhofe, and Rounds.
The action history shows no committee hearing, markup, or floor vote after the referral; the bill never advanced before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau kept its authority over banks, credit card issuers, payday lenders, and debt collectors, and borrowers kept the federal recourse the agency provides. The firms that would have gained from its repeal got nothing.

sides.party_line_note: All 8 senators behind the bill (1 sponsor plus 7 cosponsors) were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never reached a vote so no roll call exists.

industries.note: Repeal would end CFPB supervision and enforcement over credit cards, checking accounts, and overdraft practices, where the bureau has ordered refunds of fees. The industry's gain — freedom from rules and penalties — comes directly out of borrowers' protections.

The CFPB was the first federal regulator to write rules limiting repeated high-cost lending, and repeal would remove that threat. These lenders profit when the rules restricting them are off the table.

The bureau brings more collection complaints and enforcement cases than any other federal agency; repeal would end that oversight. Collectors gain by removing scrutiny of their practices toward ordinary debtors.

Repeal unwinds the Dodd-Frank title that gave the bureau authority over mortgage origination and servicing rules, reducing compliance obligations. Servicers gain; borrowers lose servicing and foreclosure protections.
